title: PEARL: Training Socratic Tutors with Pedagogically Aligned Reinforcement Learning

paper.title: PEARL: Training Socratic Tutors with Pedagogically Aligned Reinforcement Learning
paper.abstract: Abstract Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown promise as educational tutors, yet effective tutoring requires more than solving problems: it must provide progressive Socratic guidance and balance multiple pedagogical objectives across multi-turn interactions. However, training such tutors remains challenging due to limited-fidelity and weakly controllable student simulation, under-specified pedagogical reward modeling, and unstable multi-objective optimization. To overcome these limitations, we propose PEARL, a pe dagogically a ligned r einforcement l earning framework for training Socratic tutoring agents, consisting of three key components. First, we introduce a controllable student simulator that decouples latent cognitive states from response generation to model diverse abilities and misconceptions. Second, we develop a generative reward model that jointly evaluates pedagogical quality and objective correctness for policy optimization. Finally, we propose a stable multi-objective RL scheme that discretizes rewards within each dimension and aggregates normalized advantages across dimensions, preventing high-variance objectives from dominating updates. Experiments on multiple benchmarks show that PEARL achieves the best performance among open-source models and remains competitive with leading proprietary LLMs, despite using only a 30B policy model 1 1 1 Code and prompts are available at: https://github.com/JingMog/PEARL .

Figure 1: Overview of the guided tutoring task and its challenges. (a) Guided teaching elicits student reasoning through Socratic interaction. (b) Training such tutors requires controllable simulation, holistic evaluation, and stable multi-objective RL. 1 Introduction In recent years, Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable progress in reasoning, self-reflection, and generalization ( Yang et al., 2025 ; Bai et al., 2025 ) . With capabilities such as multi-turn dialogue, planning, memory augmentation, and tool invocation, LLM-based agents have shown strong potential across numerous domains ( Team et al., 2026 ; Zeng et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2025a ; Chang et al., 2026 ) . Among these applications, education has emerged as a particularly promising area due to its reliance on interactive dialogue and reasoning-intensive problem solving ( Létourneau et al., 2025 ) . Educational agents aim to support students through one-on-one, multi-turn dialogue guided by pedagogical principles ( Vajjala et al., 2025 ) . However, strong problem-solving ability does not automatically translate into effective teaching. Effective tutors must move beyond answer dumping and adopt Socratic strategies that diagnose students’ knowledge gaps and provide progressive, scaffolded hints ( Hu et al., 2025 ) . Developing such pedagogical intuition remains a central challenge for LLM-based tutoring systems. Although recent studies have made meaningful progress in AI tutors ( Shi et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2025b ; Wang et al., 2025 ) , training high-quality tutoring agents with RL still faces three core bottlenecks: limited-fidelity student simulation, under-specified pedagogical reward modeling, and unstable multi-objective optimization . (1) For student simulation , existing student simulators typically prompt LLMs to role-play students ( Macina et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2024a ; Dinucu-Jianu et al., 2025 ) , sometimes with additional student profiles for diversity ( Liu et al., 2024b ; Gao et al., 2025 ) . However, they usually generate responses end-to-end without explicitly modeling students’ cognitive states or decision-making processes, limiting their ability to capture diverse misconceptions, partial understandings, and evolving learning dynamics, which creates a fidelity gap for tutor training. (2) For pedagogical reward modeling , existing evaluations either rely on costly human annotation ( Macina et al., 2023 ) or adopt LLM-as-a-judge frameworks ( Wei et al., 2025 ; Song et al., 2025 ) . However, these signals are often insufficient for RL optimization: they lack fine-grained trajectory-level scoring criteria, and rarely jointly assess pedagogical effectiveness and objective correctness. (3) For multi-objective optimization , pedagogical tutoring involves multiple competing objectives, yet prior approaches often compute terminal rewards via simple averaging ( Song et al., 2025 ) . Because evaluation metrics differ substantially in variance scales and reward sparsity, high-variance objectives can dominate gradient updates under policy-gradient methods such as GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) and PPO ( Schulman et al., 2017 ) , hindering balanced optimization across instructional goals. To address these challenges, we propose PEARL, a pe dagogically a ligned r einforcement l earning framework for training Socratic tutoring agents. PEARL enhances the tutoring capability of LLMs through three components: simulation environment design, reward modeling, and training algorithms. (1) For student simulation , we design a controllable student simulator with cognition-decision decoupling that explicitly models students’ learning abilities. By separating cognitive priors from the generation process, it enables more diverse and controllable simulation of student misconceptions and learning dynamics, reducing fidelity gaps. (2) For pedagogical reward modeling , we develop a generative reward model for tutoring dialogue assessment. It jointly evaluates pedagogical effectiveness and objective correctness, while producing interpretable rationales and reward signals for RL optimization. (3) For multi-objective optimization , we propose a stable multi-objective RL scheme that discretizes rewards within each dimension to denoise noisy signals, and aggregates normalized advantages across dimensions to prevent high-variance objectives from dominating updates. We evaluate PEARL on multiple benchmarks across diverse educational difficulty levels, including GSM8K ( Cobbe et al., 2021 ) , MATH-500 ( Hendrycks et al., 2021 ) , MathTutorBench ( Macina et al., 2025 ) , and MathDial ( Macina et al., 2023 ) . Experimental results show that PEARL, despite using only a 30B policy model, achieves the best performance among open-source models and remains competitive with proprietary LLMs. Our primary contributions are as follows: • We propose a cognition-decision decoupled student simulator that explicitly models students’ learning ability, enabling controllable simulation of student learning behaviors. • We develop a generative reward model that turns pedagogical principles into executable reward criteria, jointly capturing pedagogical effectiveness and objective correctness. • We introduce a multi-objective RL optimization scheme that combines reward discretization and advantage aggregation to achieve balanced optimization across multiple objectives. • Experiments on multiple benchmarks demonstrate that PEARL achieves the best performance among open-source models. 2 Methodology Figure 2: Overview of the controllable student simulator: (a) knowledge decomposition, (b) modeling the student’s latent cognitive state, and (c) generating responses with behavior prediction and consistency checking. 2.1 PEARL Overview and Problem Formulation We consider the problem of training a Socratic tutoring agent in multi-turn tutoring interactions, as shown in Figure 1 . Unlike standard question answering, Socratic tutoring requires not only producing correct solutions but also delivering progressive guidance that helps students develop understanding step by step. To this end, we formulate PEARL as a closed-loop framework consisting of three components: controllable student simulation for interactive environment construction, generative reward modeling for pedagogically aligned reward estimation, and pedagogically aligned tutor optimization for policy learning. Formally, given a problem instance q q , a tutoring episode τ \tau is represented as a multi-turn trajectory τ = ( q , u 1 , a 1 , u 2 , a 2 , … , u t , a t , … , u n , a n ) , \displaystyle\tau=(q,u^{1},a^{1},u^{2},a^{2},...,u^{t},a^{t},...,u^{n},a^{n}), (1) where u t u^{t} and a t a^{t} denote the student and tutor utterances at turn t t , respectively, and n n is the total number of turns. After the dialogue terminates, the full trajectory τ \tau is evaluated by a judge model π judge \pi_{\text{judge}} , which produces a K K -dimensional reward vector 𝐫 ⁡ ( τ ) = [ r 1 ​ ( τ ) , r 2 ​ ( τ ) , … , r K ​ ( τ ) ] . \displaystyle\mathbf{r}(\tau)=[r_{1}(\tau),r_{2}(\tau),...,r_{K}(\tau)]. (2) PEARL then optimizes the tutor policy π θ \pi_{\theta} to achieve strong performance across these objectives. The remainder of this section details the three components of PEARL: controllable student simulation (Section 2.2 ), generative reward modeling (Section 2.3 ), and pedagogically aligned tutor optimization (Section 2.4 ). 2.2 Controllable Student Simulation Effective tutor training requires interaction with students exhibiting diverse abilities, misconceptions, and learning behaviors. However, existing LLM-based role-playing simulators encode student characteristics only implicitly, leading to limited controllability and weak cognitive grounding. To address this, we introduce explicit cognition modeling: instead of directly generating student responses, our simulator first represents what the student knows and how the student tends to reason, and then uses these latent cognitive states to guide response generation. Specifically, we decouple student simulation into knowledge decomposition, latent cognitive state modeling, and response generation, as illustrated in Figure 2 . Knowledge Decomposition. Given a problem q q , we decompose it into a set of structured knowledge units, such as integer arithmetic and equation solving, and organize them into a knowledge network according to prerequisite relations. This network provides an explicit representation of the knowledge structure required for solving the problem. For a student at turn t t , we denote the mastery states over these units as 𝐦 t \mathbf{m}^{t} . By assigning different mastery states to different students, the simulator can explicitly control variations in knowledge mastery. Latent Cognitive State Modeling. Beyond what the student knows, effective simulation also requires modeling how the student engages with tutoring. We therefore introduce a latent cognitive profile 𝐜 \mathbf{c} to characterize student-level cognitive and behavioral tendencies, including activeness, learning perseverance, comprehension ability, expressive ability, and attention.
